Name: -1_horses_plow_horse_servant
Representative_Docs:
["Little boy, young lad,  
When you go to courtship  
To meet the maiden,  
Put on a silk shirt,  
A silk shirt, a golden hood,  
Blue ribbons on your shoulder,  
Invite me to the sheepfold.  
Go to the church road,  
All the high ones go on the church road,  
The fools go among other people,  
Follow the path behind the scythe's blade,  
Go to the hay arch,  
Watch from the corner of the barn,  
Then you will get a wife who is broad-shouldered,  
With a cross on her chest,  
She knows how to manage the household,  
She makes the bed without sparks,  
She cooks broth without bitterness,  
She milks the cow without a chandelier,  
But she knows how to handle  
To hit the children softly,  
To make the family neat,  
She weaves patterns into fabrics,  
Diamond shapes into rings,  
Ram horns on the outer edges,  
Calf horns in the middle,  
Goat horns in the center,  
Hoof horns at the back end.  
If you don’t go to the church road,  
She doesn’t know how to manage,  
She just goes to bed,  
Places her feet against the wall,  
Her bare feet on the table.  
Oh, my dear mutual companion,  
Help me to the oven,  
Lift me onto the stove.  
From there I roll like a log,  
A half-filled bottle of beer.", "Others went early to Tiole  
I go to Iljapeal to fetch  
I hope for the stallion's strength  
For the stallion’s full step  
For the mare’s gait by Kõrvi.  
The stallion did no plowing for me  
The mare didn’t plow the wet earth  
The stallion didn’t wet the rye stalks.  
Surely that lout forced me  
To plow the start of the land  
Wet land by the hill's edge  
Swamp mud by the bog’s edge  
Still, I plowed a piece in defiance  
I left one furrow for the field  
Plowed one, left another  
Then I got ahead of the others  
By the time of the Tiopäev hearing  
Waiting for food to be brought  
For the white bucket to be carried  
But I saw food being brought  
For the black bucket to be carried  
Immediately my heart fell sad  
My heart started to ache  
Look at the thing I was given  
The food that was brought to me  
The middle grew cold  
Velvetfully listed  
Burnt bread crusts:  
I pick them up and get angry  
Scatter the chaff on the grass  
Scatter the chaff in the yard corner  
I stuck the whip into the corner  
I struck the walls of the sauna  
I myself went to Aru tavern  
Took a few shots of vodka  
Two handfuls from the jug  
A strong mug of beer  
I felt my legs turning  
My legs weakening  
Surely the legs will lead home  
The calves will go to the bed  
The knees will put themselves to sleep  
The soles of the feet into the bed.", 'Mai fed me for dinner  
Maie kept watch until midnight  
When I fell asleep  
She killed the singing bird from the barn  
Killed the black rooster from the meadow  
From the street, a little lamb  
From the market, a white-headed calf  
Morning came out white  
Mother-in-law goes upstairs shouting  
Rise, Maie, my dear one  
Maie immediately understands, hears  
Cannot rise, cannot wake  
The misty blankets are lost  
The covers are torn differently  
Mother-in-law immediately understands, hears  
Why did you kill the cruel companion  
The cruel companion, the dreamed man  
I killed the singing bird from the barn  
From the street, a little lamb  
From the market, a white-headed calf  
Maie comes up to dress  
Puts on a blue silk  
Around the waist a rose-patterned belt  
On the head, a red wreath  
Mai puts a mark in the tuft of grass  
A scar in the garden stick  
A cross in the rings of Riga  
Beloved, dear one  
Sweetheart, companion  
If you come looking for me  
Take the marks from the tuft of grass  
The scars from the garden stick  
The crosses from the rings of Riga  
Then come looking for me  
Give strength to the gray horse  
Give the boat appropriate power  
Then come looking for me  
Sparks struck the shad fish’s legs  
Kicks struck the foal’s thighs  
The maiden, entering the stable  
The maiden rushing into the stall  
Row to that city below,  
Where there are three maidens  
The first has pearls on her neck  
The last has a tag on her neck  
In between, there are poor children  
At the top, there are slave children  
They see the fire coming  
Shouting by the chandelier  
Spinning without nails  
To the pain of the night, to the pain of the moon  
The night’s pain milks the cow  
The moon’s pain strains the milk  
The pain of the bull’s head in the barn  
The beauty of the colorful gloves']

Name: 0_hay_little grandmother_granny_mourning
Representative_Docs:
["Our two poor peasants  
Let's go to Midsummer at the church  
Let's go to the grandmother's grave  
Let's go to the grandfather's grave  
Put the sorrow handkerchiefs on  
Put the sorrow apples in the handkerchief  
Rise up, little grandmother  
Rise up, little grandfather  
Rise up to braid my hair  
To prepare the grain container  
To fasten the coffin lid.  
But the woman answered, the man replied  
You cannot rise, young daughter  
You cannot rise, do not wake up  
Grass had grown over the soil  
Branch hay over the grave  
Coltsfoot on the eyebrows  
Bluebells on the eyes  
Marigolds at the feet.  
Still rise, little grandmother  
Still rise, little grandfather  
Rise up to braid my hair.  
I feed grass to the calves  
Hay to the oxen  
Coltsfoot to the roosters  
Bluebells to the pigs  
Marigolds to the calves.", "Our Two Poor Children  
Let's go to the Midsummer Day church  
Let's go to grandmother's grave;  
Let's go to grandfather's grave.  
Rise up, dear grandmother,  
Rise up, dear grandfather,  
Rise to comb my hair,  
To prepare Annivakka,  
To fasten the coffin lid.  

You must not rise, young daughter,  
You must not rise, do not awaken.  
Grass has grown over the soil,  
Field herbs upon the grave,  
Bluebells on the eyes,  
Coltsfoot on the eyebrows,  
Marsh marigold at the feet,  
Wild berries on the toes.  

You must not rise, young daughter,  
You must not rise, do not awaken.  
May God comb your hair,  
May He prepare Annivakka.  
Still rise, dear grandmother,  
I will feed the grass to the calves,  
Field herbs to the oxen,  
Bluebells to the cows.  

Oh, our two poor children,  
Let's go to the Midsummer Day church.  
I am going to grandmother's grave,  
You are going to grandfather's grave.  

Rise up, dear grandfather,  
Rise up, dear grandmother,  
Rise to comb my hair,  
To prepare Annivakka,  
To fasten the coffin lid.  

But grandmother understood and grandfather answered:  
Grass has grown over the soil,  
Field herbs upon the grave,  
Coltsfoot on the eyebrows,  
Bluebells on the eyes,  
Marsh marigolds at the feet.  

Still rise, dear grandfather,  
Still rise, dear grandmother.  
I will feed the grass to the calves,  
Field herbs to the oxen,  
Coltsfoot to the roosters,  
Bluebells to the pigs,  
Marsh marigold to the calves.", 'Our two mourners  
Let's go to the midsummer church  
Handkerchiefs in hand  
Mourning cloths on the head  
One cries, the other cries  
One wipes the other's eyes  
One strokes the other's head  
Let's go to grandmother's grave  
Let's go to grandfather's grave  
"Rise up, little grandmother,  
Rise to comb my head,  
To prepare the gift basket,  
To fasten the kerchief."  
"You must not rise, young daughter,  
You must not rise, do not awaken:  
Grass has grown over the soil,  
Hay grown over the grave;  
Apple trees over the straw,  
Bluebells over the eyes,  
Coltsfoot over the eyebrows,  
Linden trees over the hair.  
Feed the grass to the young bullocks,  
The hay to the oxen,  
The bluebells to the cows."  
"Still rise, little grandmother;  
I will bring a sand sieve from the town,  
From the market, a fine sieve,  
From the borough, a coarse sieve,  
I would sift the sieve with fine grains,  
Roll it with fine sand."  
The grandmother hears, replies:  
"You must not rise, do not awaken,  
May God comb your head,  
May the Creator fasten your kerchief,  
Prepare the gift basket."  
"Then I go home crying:  
A speckled bird was on the kerchief,  
A white bird was on the basket.  
I would like to thank:  
To God for grandmother's soul,  
To God for grandfather's soul,  
Hands into Mary's hands,  
Heart into Jesus' lap,  
Knees into the Creator's earth."']

Name: 1_sheep_went barn_cow_plowing
Representative_Docs:
['I traveled a bit in Turkey  
A hundred versts in Germany,  
A little on the road to Narva  
Half a verst in Finland.  
I did not see the wonder  
That I saw in Näo village.  
Bulls were barking, dogs were plowing,  
Cats were weaving fabric.  
The pig went to work, the sickle was on the belt,  
The fox traveled with reins around its neck.  
The horse brought a young bull calf,  
The cow brought a clump of grass,  
The sheep went to the table to lay eggs.  
The hen brought two lambs,  
Girls made sledges,  
Women spun spinning wheels,  
Men walked the path of straws.', 'Once I traveled to Turkey,  
A bit to Narva land,  
Half a mile to Poland,  
I didn’t see the wonder,  
That I saw in my village,  
In my Otsaje household:  
Bulls were barking, dogs were plowing,  
The sheep went to the barn to lay eggs,  
The hen brought two lambs,  
The cow brought a calf of the meadow.  
The horse was a bull-calf,  
The girls were making weddings,  
The women were chopping wheel wood,  
The men were walking the tavern road.', "What's wrong with us drinking at the tavern
My ox mows the home hay.
My cow takes a rest at home.
The pig makes slender bread.
But the rooster pecks in the enclosure.
The sheep is in the barn on a penny.
Oh, wonder, see the wonder
What I saw in Näu village
The oxen barked, the dogs plowed
The oxen barked at the ram
The dogs plowed at the he-goat
The horse got a bull calf
The cow gave birth to a colt
The rooster went to the barn to lay eggs
The hen went to crow more
The sheep gave birth to a speckled goat kid
The goat gave birth to a colt lamb."]

Name: 2_village swing_brothers swing_swing_swing smiths
Representation: ['village swing', 'brothers swing', 'swing', 'swing smiths', 'swing swing', 'swings', 'swinging', 'dear birch', 'village girls', 'pasture']
Representative_Docs:
['Where has our swing been brought from?  
Where has it been brought from, where has it been obtained?  
Who is bringing our swing,  
Who is bringing it, who is receiving it?  
Toomas is bringing, Sander is receiving.  
The beams were brought from Arjamaa,  
The shaft was brought from Võhmuta,  
The steps from Sinisalu.  
So a new swing was made,  
Will this swing carry us?  
If it does not carry, let it perish.  
Swing smiths, eldest brothers,  
Bring fire, burn the swing,  
Bring water, soak the swing,  
You yourself, hew the swing frame.  
Come, women of the swing village,  
Bring chickens, bring eggs,  
Bring vessels for weaving,  
Bring a pair of ducks;  
The hen stayed at home to lay eggs,  
The rooster stayed at the yard crowing.', "Let's go swing on the swing,  
Sing songs on the baseboard.  
Swing smiths, gentle brothers,  
The swing moves high along,  
The boyfriend’s swing moves softly.  
Swing smiths, gentle brothers,  
Let me down, I would ask.  
If you won’t let me down, don’t ask either.  
I will wait until evening,  
Swing until the middle of the morning,  
Sing until broad daylight.  
Surely the spruce yields milk,  
Surely the alder milks the cow,  
Surely the birch guides the herd,  
The maple tree waters the calf.  
Mund’s herd is far away,  
Mund’s heifers are in the meadow.  
Our herd is in the pasture,  
Our heifers are in the mud,  
Our sheep are in the barn,  
The geese are still in the fodder.", "Come to the swing, village girls  
Bring chickens, bring eggs  
Bring geese for hatching  
Bring ducks for brooding  
Ten girls in the village  
Nine across the street  
The tenth, the smith's daughter of the village  
They were allowed to come to the swing  
Afraid the gold would wear out  
The silver beads fade away  
The bright eyes grow pale  
There were many swinging on the swing  
Many swaying on the swing’s beam  
There are no singers on the swing  
No ones singing on the swing plank  
I praise the swing frame  
May the swing-makers be healthy  
Who made the swing to the berry hill  
Among the blue flowers  
In the red alder growing  
Between the beautiful birches  
Kind swing-makers, dear brothers  
Please let it down for me  
If you don’t let it down, I won’t ask  
Then I’ll sway till evening  
Swing till midday  
Surely then the young woman will milk the cow  
Surely then the old man will drive the herd  
If the young woman does not milk the cow  
Nor the old man drives the herd  
Surely then the alder will milk the cow  
Surely then the birch will drive the herd  
The maple tree will give water to the calf  
I hear the village swinging  
Singing on the swing plank  
Waiting for the crowd to call out  
Afraid the crowd will shout  
The crowd does not call me out  
Nor does the crowd shout at me."]

Name: 3_ends_field little_harvest_cutting
Representative_Docs:
['End, end, little field  
Come to an end, little island  
Chop, dear little clearing  
You have long been for chopping  
Every day people walked on you  
Every noon you were cut  
Every hour people came near  
Long ago I cooked chopped porridge  
Long ago chop or it melts  
Still chop, not yet cut  
To Attüma’s father  
To Attüma’s mother  
To feed and to water  
Well to send off  
Fed us with pork  
From the share of the kohioin  
To the tassel of the ox’s head  
What I promised to father  
What I promised to mother  
Tubs full, boxes full  
Children’s wide bellies full  
A thousand measures for the windy foot  
A hundred measures for the horn-stock  
Even more for father.', 'End, end, little field  
Come to an end, little island  
You have long been started.  
And long ago they began cutting you  
Every day they came to you.  
Every hour they came to your roots  
Rise up, sisters, truly  
Hold up the anger because  
We swim to the ends  
We reach the island’s edge  
The red beer is finished  
There are milk cakes in the barn.  
There are slender breads on the island  
So let me say it again  
Let me sing the words back.  
Maybe the slave whip is at an end  
There is a slave whip in the barn  
There are slave pains on the island.', 'End, end, little field  
Come to an end, little island  
Diminish, diminish, go away  
For you have long been cut down  
Long ago cut down, dried out  
Every day they walked on you  
Every hour they came to you  
Come, come, little wind  
Blessing, dear Creator’s wind  
Take the water from the grain  
The dew from the oat stalk  
Rust from the top of the grass  
So that I may reap a sheaf of grain  
Two sheaves with dew  
Three sheaves with the dawn.']

if my doing were otherwise

and ladies into little sticks.  
Kilts beneath wedges  
young men in front as stories.

for another my doing.

young ladies into headscarves,

myself at the back calling out:

lift the earth a little,  
turn the earth a little."', 'If it were up to me

Name: 5_dung_little bird_reeds_spruce
Representative_Docs:
['Liiri-lõõri sparrow,  
piiri-pääri swallow,  
where was your golden nest?  
In the forest on top of a dry spruce.  
Where did that dry spruce come from?  
An old man cut it down.  
Where did that old man’s father come from?  
The old man died.  
Where was that old man’s grave?  
In the long field’s garden.  
Where did the long field’s garden come from?  
Driven oxen plowed it up.  
Where did those driven oxen come from?  
A bear tore the driven oxen apart.  
Where did that bear’s father come from?  
The bear ran into the reeds.  
Where did those reeds come from?  
The sickle whistled down.  
Where did that sickle come from?  
It wore out its blade.  
Where did that blade come from?  
A hen rummaged in the dung.  
Where did that hen come from?  
A kite carried the hen over the sea.  
Where did that kite come from?  
The kite went to town.  
Where did that town come from?  
The town burned down.  
Where did the town’s ashes go?  
The wind blew them away.', 'Lõõri-lõõri little bird,  
Pääri-pääri little swallow,  
Where is your golden nest?  
In the forest on a dry spruce.  
Where did the dry spruce come from?  
An old man cut the dry spruce.  
Where did the old man come from?  
The old man died.  
Where was he buried?  
In a long field garden,  
Where did the field garden come from?  
Plowing bulls plowed it up.  
Where did the plowing bulls come from?  
A bear tore the plowing bulls apart.  
Where did the bear come from?  
The bear crawled into the reeds.  
Where did the reeds come from?  
A sickle mowed the reeds.  
Where did the sickle come from?  
A blade wore down the sickle.  
Where did the blade come from?  
A hen scratched in the manure.  
Where did the hen come from?  
A hawk snatched the hen away.  
Where did the hawk come from?  
The hawk flew over the sea.', 'Liiri-lõõri little flute  
Piiri-pääri little swallow  
Where is your golden nest?  
In the forest on a dry fir tree  
Where did that dry fir come from?  
An old man cut the fir down  
Where did that old man come from?  
The old man died  
Where was he buried?  
In the long bed of the field  
Where did that field bed come from?  
Oxen plowed it up  
Where did those oxen come from?  
A bear broke them down  
Where did that bear come from?  
The bear went to the long reeds  
Where did those reeds come from?  
A sickle mowed them down  
Where did that sickle come from?  
A hoe chopped it down  
Where did that hoe come from?  
A hen scratched in the manure  
Where did that hen come from?  
A hawk broke it down  
Where did that hawk come from?  
A Saxon shot it down  
Where did that Saxon come from?  
The Saxon went to town  
Where did that town come from?  
The town burned down  
Where did that fire come from?  
Water put it out  
Where did that water come from?  
The water ran into the sea  
Where did that sea come from?  
The sea grew into black land.']

Name: 6_beers_hops_drink beer_hop
Representative_Docs:
["In the hollow, a pine cone calls into the stream  
A cone crackles into the bush  
In the grassy rye field  
Come here, young men  
Take me to the sack at home  
Set me on the bench by the stove  
Put me on the board to dry  
From there I roll into the cellar  
But I slip into the half-beer glass  
Drift into the beer mug  
Sink into the beer anchor  
Make me a good beer  
That takes away men's senses  
Half of the senses from the boys' heads  
Thanks to wise women's heads  
Men grumble without hats  
Women dance without cloth  
Girls without belts  
Boys with crooked backs  
One drinks from one hand to the other  
Mothers-in-law, mothers with buckets  
Look, I drink from the pail  
I feed my head through the pipe  
Do I drink from the cupboard, or from the jug  
Or do I drink from the colorful cup  
The cone makes the eyes colorful  
The jug makes the neck stiff.", 'The hop drifts to the mountain valley,  
The cone crackles in the oven’s hearth:  
Come here, young men,  
Take me to the barrel’s home,  
Carry me to the cellar house,  
Put me on the edge of the board,  
From there I roll into the cask,  
I slip into the half-pint of beer,  
I make the cask whistle,  
The beers rise on the straw -  
Then I take the senses from the heads of men,  
The drifts go to the ends of women,  
Half of the senses from the heads of boys;  
Then the men shout without hats,  
The women danced without a tanuta*,  
Boys in half-boots,  
Girls with wreaths on their heads.  

*Note: "tanuta" is an Estonian folk dance or festive term that has no direct English equivalent.', "A little beer, a little beauty,  
A little ale, a little darling,  
From your face, you are the handsome one,  
From your stomach, you are the sweet one.  
You walk along my stomach,  
March along my belly,  
Stretch along the spine.  
Be healthy, brewers!  
Who made good beer,  
Often went to the tavern,  
Sometimes went to the well.  
But I sip along with my mind,  
I try along the edge of the pitcher.  
The hop calls in the stream,  
The cone crackles in the bush:  
Come, come young men,  
Pick me into your sack,  
Take me out for the work in the field,  
Put me on the bench edge,  
Carry me to the kitchen stove!  
Then I rise onto the loft,  
I swell along the long gutter.  
Then I take the minds of men,  
Half the minds of the boys' heads,  
The temples from the women's foreheads.  
Men make noise without hats,  
Women dance without shoes,  
Boys half kneeling.  
The beer was wild and the bottle was smart,  
Ale was very sly.  
Oh, you proud barley water,  
Oh, you wrathful grain water,  
Though you surely bring me down,  
Still, I take you inside me."]

Tasted our well water  
Tasted Mardi's grayish one

I went to take a drink,  
I took one drink, I took two,

Name: 57_cattle_livestock_pasture_weaving
Representative_Docs:
["The wind comes, the bonfire sings

I keep the old woman's sheep  
I protect the old man's spotted cattle  
In front of God's house  
Behind Marie's room  
Between the creator's barns  
Go to the herd, blue herd  
Put (them) to the herd, red herd  
Let the herd rest  
Let them rest for a moment  
To wither into a little scrap  
Until I tie the leg bands  
Fastening the shoe laces  
Weaving the old woman's apron strings  
Beating the bark straps  
I drive in the old scatterings  
I create the old woman's swirls  
I knit cat paw shapes.", "Eat the cattle, blue cattle  
Drink the cattle, red cattle  
Old woman's cattle, Ingamaa  
For a little while, to wander  
For an hour, to take a nap  
Until I tie the shoe laces  
Fastening the shoe laces  
I weave the old woman's apron ribbon  
Under the apron, a little garden  
On the apron, a little ribbon  
I make a pattern on the belt  
I touch the cat's paw pattern  
I weave on the shirt's tail  
I make holes in the weaving  
I put ribbons into the work  
I insert the ends of the frame.", 'Eat, cattle, blue cattle  
Drink, cattle, red cattle  
Lie down, cattle, to rest

To cool down a bit

Until I set the pig ropes  
Weave grandmother’s apron strings

Eat, cattle, blue cattle  
Drink, cattle, red cattle  
Lie down, cattle, to rest  
To rest during the heat

The pasture to go seek  
In the foggy morning  
In the rough dew  
On the cloudy days

Into the dense bush

Name: 58_barking_goats_goat_went barn
Representative_Docs:
["Oh, poor Tõnu of the herd
I always received harsh words.
The wolf ate many sheep
And the goats from Kiviääre. -
My father-in-law was very rich,
My mother-in-law was very rich.
I was once rich from the cross,
And even richer from the godfather,
He took me to Riga for baptism
And to give me a name in Tallinn.
He gave me a little goat,
A bell for the goat's neck.
The wolf ate the goat—the bell remained with me.
I put the bell around the woman’s neck,
The woman dozed off, the bell jingled.
The woman was a heavy sleeper,
The bell made an even louder noise.", "I had a rich godmother  
a rich godfather  
they gave me a little goat  
a little bell around the goat's neck  
then came the wolf in a mad mood  
took the goat, the bell stayed with me.  
I put the bell on the dog's neck  
but the dog barked, the bell clanged.  
Then came the wolf in a mad mood  
took the dog, the bell stayed with me.  
I put the bell on the hen's neck  
but the hen cackled, the bell clanged.  
Then came the hawk in a mad mood  
took the hen, the bell stayed with me.  
I put the bell on the wife's neck  
but the wife groaned, the bell clanged.  
Then came Death in a mad mood  
took the wife, the bell stayed with me.  
Then I put the bell on top of the cupboard  
to mourn the old woman  
to look for the new woman.", "I had a rich godmother  
She gave me a little goat  
A little bell for the goat's neck,  
A little bell for the goat's neck.  
But a wolf took that goat away  
I put the bell on the dog's neck  
The dog was barking, the bell was ringing,  
The dog was barking, the bell was ringing.  
But the wolf took that dog away  
I put the bell on the wife's neck  
The wife was loud and sleepy  
The bell was loud and banging  
Come now, come now, young maiden  
Come now dance with me  
Come now, come now, the bagpipe is playing  
So does my heart then  
What harm is there in living  
To enjoy the bachelor’s days  
The rooster went to the barn to eat the grain  
The hen went into the sack to rest  
The elk went into the forest to cut hay  
The cow went to fetch feed  
Is this pipe following the foot  
Or is this man following the heart"]

Name: 63_rains_harju_harjumaa_rain
Representative_Docs:
['Over, over the rain stream,  
Over the ditch I wait,  
Enduring the dewdrop stream.  
Bring the rain towards Vigala,  
Drive the rain towards Arju,  
Bring Vigala cattle to drink,  
And Ugala to drink as well,  
To wash the hands of Arju women,  
To wash the hands, to wash the dirt.  
In Arju land the men are dark,  
Men are dark, women are rude,  
Boys like burnt stumps,  
Girls like tar stumps; -  
In our land the men were fine,  
Men were fine, boys were strong,  
Girls were fire-beautiful.  
Over, over the rain stream,  
Over the ditch I wait,  
Enduring the dewdrop stream.  
Why rain should come short,  
What use do we have without dew?  
I do not sow in the rain,  
Nor rot in the wet,  
I do not grow without dew.  
Grain sprouts with rain,  
Grass rots in the wet,  
Oats grow with dew.', 'Over, over, rain showers!  
Over the shower, I wait.  
I endure the dew shower.  
Take the rain to Vigala land,  
Send the rain to Harju land,  
For the cattle of Vigala to drink,  
For the women of Harju to wash their hands,  
To wash their hands, to wash their scarves.  
In Harju land the men are dark,  
Men are dark, women are dark,  
Girls fiery,  
Boys with curly hair,  
Children like little flames.  
In our land the men are fair,  
Men are fair, women are fair,  
Girls very beautiful,  
Boys with golden hair,  
Children like cowslips.', 'Go over the rain showers,  
Over the showers, I wait,  
Carrying dew to the ankles.  
Over these diligent times,  
Over these frequent rains,  
Over dark clouds,  
Over harsh heavy burdens.  
Take the rain toward Vigala,  
Scatter the rain toward Harju,  
Carry the rain to the distant places.  
For the cattle of Vigala to drink,  
For the women of Harju to wash their hands,  
To wash their hands, to wash the kerchief.  
In Harju County the men were dark,  
Men were dark, women dark,  
Boys half were dark-skinned.  
In our land the men were white,  
Men were white, women white,  
Boys half were Saxons.']
